source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum, Goodman (2012) Bootstrapping in a language of thought
finding: A Bayesian learner over lambda-calculus programs (set, logic, count-list primitives) goes through one-, two-, three-, four-knower stages and then jumps to a recursive counting program, as children do.
numbers: Hypothesis space is all compositions of the primitives; CHILDES numeral frequencies as data; hypotheses inspected at 200 data points; results hold across settings of the two free parameters (noise, cost of recursion).
limits: Timing of the jump is not predicted: it depends on a free parameter for recursion cost and on the chosen primitives. Fit to children is qualitative, with no fit statistic.
agent_relevance: A concept can be represented as a short program and learned by a posterior over programs; the jump to a general rule happens only when data exceed what simpler special cases explain.

source: Piantadosi et al. (2012), what the model needs and how it can fail
finding: The model does not build in successor or Mod-N. Removing doubleton and tripleton primitives makes the jump earlier; adding quadrupleton and quintupleton delays it. A different count-list order (alphabetical) would block the jump.
numbers: Informal primitive manipulations only; no systematic sweep reported.
quote: key for explaining why children make the correct CP inference
limits: The authors say the model could be refuted if children compute Mod-N as easily as small-set operations. Result depends on the hand-picked primitive set.
agent_relevance: The primitive set decides what is learnable and when. The choice of operators is a first-order design decision, not a detail.

source: Piantadosi et al. (2012), critique and rival account
finding: Carey's bootstrapping says the jump comes from analogy over the early words; the model says it comes only from evidence that simpler special cases cannot explain. The model predicts a child who hears only the first three number words never makes the jump.
numbers: No new child experiment is reported. Rips, Asmuth and Bloomfield (as discussed in the paper) argue a modular number system fits the same data; the model answers that Mod-N is not a primitive.
limits: Critics (Asmuth, from a search summary only) say the learned concept is not discontinuous with the starting ones. The reply holds only under the paper's own primitive choice.
agent_relevance: Hand-chosen primitives can smuggle in the answer. For our agent, an operator library must be audited the same way: what does it make trivially expressible?

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum, Goodman (2016) The logical primitives of thought
finding: Large online study: 108 Boolean and quantifier concepts, 1,596 participants, 25 sets per concept. A Bayesian program-learning model with a simplicity prior predicts held-out responses.
numbers: Best Boolean grammar (FULLBOOLEAN) explains about 88% of variance in held-out response patterns. Outlier removal dropped 3.9% of data on average (SD 2.6%). Verbal rules asked at sets 5, 10, 25.
limits: Mechanical Turk sample; verbal descriptions too ambiguous to analyse. Quantifier concepts fit worse: about 66% of response variance, 78% of concept-mean difficulty.
agent_relevance: Program-length priors predict human generalisation errors well enough to compare candidate operator sets by held-out fit.

source: Piantadosi et al. (2016), rival models and primitive sets
finding: Structured rule languages beat unstructured models. The exemplar model explains only about half the variance. A uniform prior with no simplicity bias is the next worst. Richer connectives (biconditional) beat and/or/not alone. The Horn-clause language, common in AI, did several hundred log-likelihood points worse than the top grammars.
numbers: Exemplar model about half the variance vs about 88% for the best rule language; SIMPLEBOOLEAN and NAND below FULLBOOLEAN and BICONDITIONAL.
limits: The authors say a rule model may mimic gradient effects by averaging over rules, and hybrid rule-plus-exemplar models (Nosofsky) are not ruled out. One task format only (one concept, three-feature shapes).
agent_relevance: Rules with a length penalty are a better default bias than similarity to past cases for single-concept induction. Judge by held-out generalisation, not fit to given examples (G3).

source: Piantadosi et al. (2016), individual versus group patterns
finding: Averages look graded, but single participants switch sharply, consistent with each person holding one rule at a time. Early learned rules are simplified approximations of the target.
numbers: From per-participant response rasters (Fig 5); no single test statistic.
limits: Evidence is visual and qualitative; graded-average versus rule-per-person is not formally separated.
agent_relevance: Expect an inducer to commit first to a simple wrong rule. Held-out checks must target the places where the short and the true rule disagree.

source: Goodman, Tenenbaum, Feldman, Griffiths (2008) A rational analysis of rule-based concept learning
finding: Rational Rules: Bayesian inference over a grammar of logical formulas with a prior that falls with formula length, fitted to classic Boolean concept data.
numbers: Not opened (download failed); no numbers recorded.
limits: From memory; check before use.
agent_relevance: Base model for the later primitive and LLM work in this file.

source: Feldman (2000) Minimization of Boolean complexity in human concept learning
finding: Difficulty of learning Boolean concepts follows the length of the shortest logical formula, across concept structures matched on number of positive examples.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: From memory; rival complexity measures claim better fit (see b09).
agent_relevance: A short-formula bias is a cheap prior on which hypothesis to try first.

source: Lafond, Lacouture, Mineau (2007) Complexity minimization in rule-based category learning
finding: Re-test of the shortest-formula account found it does not fully predict difficulty; other complexity measures or rule-plus-exception mixes fit better.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: From memory; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Formula length is a useful prior but not the whole story; keep a check on actual errors, not only on simplicity.

source: Ellis, Wong, Nye et al. (2020/2021) DreamCoder
finding: Library learning plus a neural recognition model solves program-induction tasks across several domains. Learned abstractions (filter, max, nth largest, sort) build on each other.
numbers: Text editing: 3.7% of 108 SyGuS tasks solved before learning, 79.6% after (10 minute limit). Best prior solver CVC4 82.4% at 1 hour, 8 CPUs; DreamCoder 84.3% at that budget. 93% of 60 physics laws learned after 8 wake-sleep cycles.
limits: Training takes about a day on 20-100 CPUs. Tasks are small, synthetic or curated.
agent_relevance: Reusable sub-routines are what make program search tractable. A memory of solved sub-goals with a guide for search is the part to copy, not the neural nets.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder, ablations
finding: Removing library learning or the recognition model lowers the held-out solve rate. Memorising solved programs without compression is worse. In LOGO graphics and tower building no ablated variant solves more than 60% while the full model reaches nearly 100%.
numbers: Mean solve time 54.1 s, median 15.0 s across domains.
limits: The authors' own ablations; no independent replication in this paper. The LILO paper (b20) reports its own DreamCoder re-run came out weaker than the number the earlier LAPS paper reported.
agent_relevance: Both parts matter: a compact library and a guide that predicts which library parts to use.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search
finding: GPT-4 proposes natural-language hypotheses, then Python programs, which are run on the training examples. This beats direct prompting on a 100-task ARC sample.
numbers: ARC (100 random tasks): direct prompting 17%; programs without hypotheses 23%; LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%; human-selected hypotheses 33%; non-LLM Icecuber search 43%. Of 49 tasks with a human-selected hypothesis, 33 (67%) gave correct programs.
limits: 100 tasks give wide error bars. Human selection is not an automated method.
agent_relevance: The abstract-hypothesis step plus code execution as the check gives a clear gain over answering directly. Hypothesis proposal is the bottleneck, not coding.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search, ablations
finding: Writing the hypothesis in language but not coding it (chain of thought) gives no gain. On easy string tasks hypotheses add nothing because plain program generation already saturates.
numbers: ARC with language-only hypotheses 19%, below 23% for programs. SyGuS: 94.3% with direct programs and 94.3% with hypotheses (CrossBeam 74.8%). Three of five failed SyGuS tasks had errors in their examples.
limits: Parsel-style decomposition helped with human hypotheses (47.5%) but hurt with model hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Do not add a language-hypothesis step on tasks that plain code generation already solves; it costs tokens (G7). The executable form carries the gain.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: iterative hypothesis refinement
finding: Models are good rule proposers when paired with a symbolic interpreter. Refinement beats plain input-output prompting on three of four datasets.
numbers: Task accuracy, IO vs refinement: ACRE 28.0 vs 45-48; MiniSCAN 0.0 vs 46.0 (T=3); List Functions 39.6 vs 52.0 (T=1) and 42.4 (T=3); MiniARC 13.8 vs 3.8-9.2 (refinement worse).
limits: MiniARC is text-only 5x5 grids where pattern matching suits direct prompting. Self-refine with the model as its own interpreter gave 0.0 on MiniSCAN.
agent_relevance: Rule proposal plus a code checker is the gain. A model-only loop with no executor does not help.

source: Qiu et al. (2024), the rule-application gap and noise
finding: The same model applies its own induced rules badly: accuracy drops from more than 80% to almost zero on MiniSCAN when the LM, not code, applies the rule. Noisy examples hurt LMs more than humans.
numbers: Examples perturbed at 12.5%, 25%, 50%. Human study on 50 tasks per dataset showed smaller relative drops than the LM.
limits: The authors say the human study did not cover every setup, so the head-to-head comparison is partial.
agent_relevance: Never trust the model to execute its own induced rule; run it in code (G2, G5). Noisy examples need an explicit tolerance rule.

source: Li, Ellis et al. (2024) Combining induction and transduction for abstract reasoning
finding: Trained induction (write a program) and transduction (predict the output) models solve different ARC problems. Induction is better at exact computation and composing concepts; transduction at fuzzy perceptual ones. Ensembling nears average-human level.
numbers: ARC validation set: best ensemble 56.75% vs average human 60.2% and best human 97.8%. ARC-Heavy: transduction with test-time training 43.25%; induction (10k samples, majority vote) 19.25%; ensemble without TTT 29.75%.
limits: Models trained on synthetic data derived from ARC training tasks. Other authors later raised the transduction score to 61.9% with better test-time training.
agent_relevance: Run a program route and a direct-answer route in parallel and let code choose by agreement on held-out checks. Neither route alone covers the task set.

source: Li et al. (2024), false-positive programs and sampling scale
finding: Induction solve rate rises almost monotonically with test-time samples. About 9% of sampled programs that fit all training examples give a wrong test output.
numbers: 9% false positives; about half of that 9% still has the correct output as the majority answer.
limits: A vote across programs removes only about half of the false positives.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3 and G4: fitting the examples is not proof; use held-out checks and vote over program outputs.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: Hypotheses written in English by an LLM, weighed by a prior tuned on human data, fit human concept learning. English hypotheses fit better than Python ones.
numbers: Number game: 50-100 sampled hypotheses fit the 8-person average; the original model used over 5000. Shape-concept data (112 concepts, 1,596 participants): 100 proposals per batch give R2 = .81 with humans and accuracy within 3% of human level, better than GPT-4 alone.
limits: The tuned prior was critical; the pretrained one is syntax-sensitive. Human data are group averages. Sampling hypotheses without looking at the data fits poorly.
agent_relevance: A language-based proposal step that looks at the data first keeps the search small. Prior weights should be tuned or checked, not left at the model default.

source: Ellis (2023), GPT-4 alone versus humans
finding: GPT-4 used directly as a judge of number-game membership gave judgements decidedly different from human averages. The Bayesian wrapper was needed for the human-like pattern.
numbers: No single figure for the number game; on the shape task GPT-4 alone has lower R2 than .81 (shown in a figure).
limits: No ground truth exists in the number game, so different is not wrong.
agent_relevance: A plain model answer is not a calibrated generaliser. Score hypotheses by evidence, not by the model's say-so.

source: Grand, Wong et al. (2024) LILO
finding: An LLM writes programs, a compressor (Stitch) finds shared sub-programs, and the LLM names them. LILO beats DreamCoder in three domains and the LLM-only solver in all three.
numbers: Over DreamCoder: REGEX +33.14, LOGO +20.42, CLEVR +2.26 (DreamCoder CLEVR already 94.50). Over the LLM solver: REGEX +0.94, CLEVR +8.09, LOGO +16.82. The LLM solver alone beats DreamCoder on REGEX by 32.20.
limits: Enumerative search adds most on LOGO. Best run and mean differ: LOGO best 73.87, mean 48.95. Their own DreamCoder re-run (28.53) was below the figure reported by the earlier LAPS paper (42.64).
agent_relevance: Gains are largest where the LLM already knows the concept (vowel). Search is still needed for structures language cannot describe.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO, the LLM as compressor
finding: Asking an LLM to do the abstraction step itself works poorly: almost no compression and mostly invalid code.
numbers: Only 19.01% (998 of 5250) of generated abstractions were valid; compression stayed near 1.0x.
limits: One prompt design and one model family.
agent_relevance: Do compression and refactoring in code; use the model only to name or explain (G5).

source: Mirchandani et al. (2023) Large language models as general pattern machines
finding: Text LLMs complete abstract token patterns in context, including part of ARC, even with arbitrary token alphabets.
numbers: ARC (800 problems): text-davinci-003 85; with random alphabets 44-46 (mean over 5); text-davinci-002 64; gpt-4-0613 77; PaLM 42; hand-built DSL search (Ainooson) 130.
limits: Authors note possible ARC contamination in training data. Numbers are not matched across models.
agent_relevance: Direct in-context completion is a non-trivial baseline that program routes must beat at equal tokens (G7).

source: Moskvichev, Odouard, Mitchell (2023) ConceptARC
finding: Humans generalise a concept across variants far better than program solvers or GPT-4.
numbers: 16 concepts, 480 test inputs. Average per-concept gap between humans and the first-place Kaggle program: 40 points. Humans above 90% on 11 of 16 concepts and above 80% on the rest. Kaggle winner never above 80%, below 60% on 11 concepts. GPT-4 below 30% on 15 of 16 concepts.
limits: Online human sample (MTurk, Prolific), about 84% per task; text-only grids for GPT-4; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Humans abstract the concept; machines tend to fit the surface. Test induction on variants of one concept, not one instance.

source: Xu, Li, Sanner, Khalil (2024) LLMs and the ARC: object-based representations
finding: GPT-4 reads ARC grids poorly as flat text. An object-based description built by an external tool raises its score.
numbers: 13/50 of the simplest ARC tasks with text grids; 23/50 with the object representation; up to 50/50 on some 1D-ARC task types.
limits: Subset of 50 easy tasks; the object extractor is itself a hand-built set of primitives.
agent_relevance: How S2 REPRESENT is formatted changes accuracy as much as the search method. Pre-process input into objects in code.

source: Kumar, Correa, Dasgupta et al. (2023) Using natural language and program abstractions to instill human inductive biases
finding: Meta-RL agents co-trained to predict human language descriptions, or library-learned program embeddings, take on a human-like bias for structured tasks. Controls (synthetic language, programs without learned primitives) do not.
numbers: Baseline agent did better on machine-made control boards than human-made boards (p < 0.0001), the opposite of humans (p < 0.0001). The language-grounded agent beat the baseline on human-like boards (p < 0.0001) and did worse on the control boards.
limits: Small neural agents on one board-task family; bootstrap tests; not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Compressing abstractions (learned primitives) carry the useful bias; plain wording does not. Favours a library of named abstractions over ad hoc hints.

source: Wong, Grand et al. (2023) From word models to world models
finding: Codex translates sentences into probabilistic programs (Church); inference over the program, not the LLM, supplies the reasoning. Shown on probabilistic, relational, physical and social reasoning.
numbers: Qualitative demonstrations only. In one worked case a program gave a person a 23.90% chance; after a contradiction the posterior dropped to 0%.
limits: No benchmark and no human comparison; the authors call their evaluations preliminary.
agent_relevance: Split the work: the model translates to a formal representation (S2) and a program does the inference. Untested at scale.
